items.title: The Lottery Year
items.question: Studies following big lottery winners find their happiness typically spikes, then drifts back near its old level within about a year. What does this suggest?
choices: Money permanently sets your happiness level
Winners secretly give all the money away
Joy from windfalls usually fades as life renormalizes
Happiness cannot be studied at all
items.correctAnswer: Joy from windfalls usually fades as life renormalizes
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — the hedonic treadmill. New circumstances thrill, then become the new normal, and happiness drifts home. Circumstances rent joy; they rarely buy it.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that joy from windfalls usually fades as life renormalizes. Winners don't stay ecstatic; ordinary days reclaim them. This is adaptation at work: minds normalize both jackpots and setbacks.
items.lessonContent:
Big wins thrill, then become background.
Minds renormalize circumstances with quiet efficiency.
Expectation, not events, sets the daily tone.
Plan for the fade before chasing the spike.
Share this: ask a friend what thrill faded fastest for them.

items.title: The Raise That Vanished
items.question: Maya's 10% raise delighted her for weeks — until it became just her salary, and she started eyeing the next bump. What happened?
choices: How her new normal swallowed the gain
Proof that raises always reduce happiness
A payroll error shrinking her checks
items.correctAnswer: How her new normal swallowed the gain
items.correctExplanation: Right. The raise reset her baseline, so the same money now feels ordinary. Treadmill logic: satisfaction tracks changes, not levels.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is how her new normal swallowed the gain. Nothing shrank except the thrill — adaptation converted a gain into background. Raises rent delight for weeks, then the lease renews at a higher price.
items.lessonContent:
Satisfaction tracks changes, not levels.
Every gain quietly reprograms what counts as normal.
The next bump is already priced into today's mood.
Savor deliberately or adaptation spends the gain for you.
Share this: recall a raise whose thrill you can no longer feel.

items.title: The New Car Smell
items.question: Leo adored his new car for a month; by season's end it was just the car. Which idea best explains the fade?
choices: New tires secretly ruin the experience
Adaptation turns thrilling upgrades into ordinary background
items.correctAnswer: Adaptation turns thrilling upgrades into ordinary background
items.correctExplanation: Yes — hedonic adaptation. The car didn't change; Leo's reference point did. Upgrades deliver a burst, then membership in the new normal.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that adaptation turns thrilling upgrades into ordinary background. The vehicle is identical; the driver renormalized. Expect the fade and you can plan around it instead of financing it.
items.lessonContent:
Upgrades deliver bursts, then background membership.
Reference points move faster than odometers.
The fade is about the perceiver, not the purchase.
Lease delight knowingly or buy experiences instead.
Share this: name a purchase that became invisible within months.

items.title: The Bigger House
items.question: The Patels upsized for happiness, felt great for a season, then started wanting the next street over. What pattern is this?
choices: The treadmill: each new normal births a new want
items.correctAnswer: The treadmill: each new normal births a new want
items.correctExplanation: Correct — the hedonic treadmill. Each arrival becomes the baseline from which the next lack is measured. Square footage can't outrun a moving reference point.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the treadmill: each new normal births a new want. The house delivered exactly what was asked, then the asking moved. Wants escalate to match means — that is the mechanism, not a housing defect.
items.lessonContent:
Arrivals become baselines; baselines breed new lacks.
Wants escalate to match means automatically.
Bigger rarely means better for long.
Contentment is a practice, not a purchase.
Share this: notice one want that grew to fit your means.

items.title: The Promotion Plateau
items.question: After months of wanting a promotion, Priya got it — and within weeks was stressed about the next level. What best describes her arc?
choices: Evidence her boss planned it cruelly
A rare medical condition of achievers
items.correctAnswer: How arrival resets ambition upward
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — arrival fallacy plus treadmill. The summit becomes base camp instantly, and ambition re-anchors higher. Achievement satisfies; it rarely satiates.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is how arrival resets ambition upward. The promotion worked — then worked itself into the background. Ambition is a horizon: walking toward it moves it. Celebrate arrivals before re-anchoring.
items.lessonContent:
Summits become base camps with startling speed.
Ambition re-anchors upward after every arrival.
Achievement satisfies; it rarely satiates.
Pause to inhabit wins before chasing sequels.
Share this: celebrate one past win you sprinted past.

items.title: The Phone Cycle
items.question: Each new phone thrills Jamal for days, then becomes the phone he complains about. What would most reliably slow this cycle?
choices: Longer gaps and gratitude for what it already does
items.correctAnswer: Longer gaps and gratitude for what it already does
items.correctExplanation: Right. Longer upgrade gaps let the baseline settle, and gratitude interrupts adaptation's erasure. You can't stop the treadmill, but you can step off the fast belt.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is longer gaps and gratitude for what it already does. Pricier phones just raise the baseline faster. Adaptation is fought with attention — noticing what works — not with specifications.
items.lessonContent:
Attention interrupts adaptation's quiet erasure.
Longer gaps let baselines settle downward.
Gratitude is treadmill resistance training.
Specifications never satisfy; noticing does.
Share this: list three things your current phone does brilliantly.

items.title: The Neighbor's Lawn
items.question: Chen was content with his car until the neighbor's gleaming SUV arrived. His car hadn't changed — what had?
choices: His reference point, now parked next door
items.correctAnswer: His reference point, now parked next door
items.correctExplanation: Correct — comparison reset his baseline. Satisfaction is relative: the same car feels poorer beside a richer signal. The Joneses live in your head rent-free.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is his reference point, now parked next door. The car is identical; the measuring stick moved. Comparison is the treadmill's engine — curate inputs and the baseline behaves.
items.lessonContent:
Satisfaction is computed against neighbors, not absolutes.
Reference points move when the street changes.
Comparison is the treadmill's engine room.
Curate what you measure yourself against.
Share this: mute one account that resets your baseline.

items.title: The Trip Afterglow
items.question: Asha's dream vacation glowed for weeks in memory, while her new sofa faded in days. What does research suggest about experiences versus things?
choices: Experiences typically resist adaptation better than possessions
items.correctAnswer: Experiences typically resist adaptation better than possessions
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Experiences become storied parts of identity and are compared less; possessions sit around inviting comparison. Money buys more lasting joy as doing than as having.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that experiences typically resist adaptation better than possessions. Trips become stories you retell; sofas become furniture you stop seeing. Comparison shopping applies to things far more than to memories.
items.lessonContent:
Doing beats having for durable delight.
Stories appreciate; objects depreciate into background.
Experiences dodge comparison — nobody benchmarks your sunset.
Spend marginal money on memory, not material.
Share this: plan one small experience instead of one upgrade.

items.title: The Grade Horizon
items.question: Sam swore a B+ would make him happy; it did for a day, then only A's would do. What shifted?
choices: His internal bar, rising to meet each win
The grading scale at his school
items.correctAnswer: His internal bar, rising to meet each win
items.correctExplanation: Right — the goalposts moved with him. Each win redefines acceptable, so satisfaction stays one step ahead. Name the bar and you can stop it drifting.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is his internal bar, rising to meet each win. The B+ didn't fail; the measuring system updated. Drifting standards guarantee permanent near-miss — unless you anchor them deliberately.
items.lessonContent:
Internal bars rise to meet every win.
Drifting standards manufacture permanent near-miss.
Name your 'enough' before the win, not after.
Satisfaction needs an anchored finish line.
Share this: write down what 'enough' means for one goal.

items.title: The Follower Count
items.question: Reaching 10,000 followers thrilled Noor for a weekend; soon only 50,000 would satisfy her. What is the healthiest reframe?
choices: Delete the app and move to the woods
Judge the work by its craft, not the counter
items.correctAnswer: Judge the work by its craft, not the counter
items.correctExplanation: Correct. Counters are pure treadmill — every milestone expires on arrival. Craft standards endure because they live outside the numbers game.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to judge the work by its craft, not the counter. Follower milestones have a half-life of days. Internal scorecards (did I make it well?) don't renormalize the way public counters do.
items.lessonContent:
Public counters expire on arrival; craft endures.
Milestones with half-lives of days are treadmills.
Internal scorecards resist renormalization.
Make for the work, count for curiosity.
Share this: praise one creator's craft, not their count.

items.title: The Expectation Tax
items.question: Two friends get identical bonuses. The one who expected double feels robbed; the one who expected nothing feels rich. What sets their joy?
choices: Expectations, taxing or gifting the same event
items.correctAnswer: Expectations, taxing or gifting the same event
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — joy equals reality minus expectations. Identical events pay different happiness depending on the forecast. Manage the forecast and you keep more of every win.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is expectations, taxing or gifting the same event. The money is equal; the surprise differs. Happiness arithmetic subtracts the forecast first — low expectations are a wealth of a kind.
items.lessonContent:
Joy equals reality minus expectations.
Forecasts tax or gift every identical event.
Expectation management is happiness budgeting.
Hope specifically, not vaguely, to calibrate well.
Share this: lower one forecast and enjoy the surplus.

items.title: The Gratitude Lever
items.question: Writing down three good things nightly reliably lifts reported well-being in studies. Why would such a tiny habit work?
choices: It tricks the brain with false memories
It redirects attention to gains adaptation would erase
It only works for naturally cheerful people
items.correctAnswer: It redirects attention to gains adaptation would erase
items.correctExplanation: Right. Adaptation erases gains from awareness; gratitude re-presents them. The habit doesn't change life — it changes what gets noticed, which is where joy lives.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that it redirects attention to gains adaptation would erase. Circumstances stay fixed; the spotlight moves. Noticing is the cheapest treadmill brake ever tested.
items.lessonContent:
Awareness is where joy actually lives.
Adaptation erases; attention restores.
Tiny nightly habits compound into baselines.
Noticing beats acquiring, daily.
Share this: text someone three good things tonight.

items.title: The Brickman Study
items.question: A 1978 study compared lottery winners, accident victims, and controls — and found all groups surprisingly close in everyday happiness. What is the core message?
choices: Humans adapt powerfully to both windfalls and misfortunes
Tragedy and fortune leave no mark at all
Controls are always the happiest group
items.correctAnswer: Humans adapt powerfully to both windfalls and misfortunes
items.correctExplanation: Correct. Both extremes drifted toward ordinary — winners down, victims up. Adaptation is symmetric: it softens tragedy and taxes triumph. Resilience is the species' default setting.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that humans adapt powerfully to both windfalls and misfortunes. The shock isn't that events don't matter — they do, intensely, at first. It's that minds pull both peaks and valleys toward the middle over time.
items.lessonContent:
Adaptation softens tragedy and taxes triumph alike.
First intensity always exceeds lasting impact.
Resilience is the default, not the exception.
Both peaks and valleys regress toward ordinary.
Share this: recall a valley you adapted out of.

items.title: The Sabbatical Test
items.question: Omar took a dream month off and felt transformed — then normal life reabsorbed him in weeks. What should he conclude?
choices: Breaks are pointless, so never rest
He rested incorrectly and should feel guilty
Lasting change needs systems, since states fade
items.correctAnswer: Lasting change needs systems, since states fade
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. States (rested, inspired) fade; systems (habits, routines) persist. The sabbatical's gift is information about what to systematize, not a permanent mood.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that lasting change needs systems, since states fade. The month worked perfectly as a diagnostic — it showed which changes matter. Import two routines home instead of mourning the vanished glow.
items.lessonContent:
States fade; systems persist.
Treat peaks as diagnostics, not destinations.
Import routines home from every escape.
Design beats inspiration over any horizon.
Share this: systematize one habit from your last break.

items.title: The Arrival Fallacy
items.question: 'I'll be happy when I land the job' — then the job lands and happiness doesn't. What error did the wish contain?
choices: Locating lasting joy in the next arrival
items.correctAnswer: Locating lasting joy in the next arrival
items.correctExplanation: Right — the arrival fallacy. Lasting joy was assigned to a future event, but events deliver bursts, not baselines. Happiness lives in practices, not arrivals.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is locating lasting joy in the next arrival. The job can satisfy without satiating — that was never its job. Assign joy to daily practices and let arrivals be pleasant weather.
items.lessonContent:
Events deliver bursts, never baselines.
'When X, then happy' mislocates joy by design.
Practices hold what arrivals only visit.
Want the job; don't invoice it for happiness.
Share this: catch yourself saying 'when X, then happy' once today.

items.title: The Variety Spice
items.question: Eating a favorite dessert daily dulled it; rotating treats kept each one special. What principle kept the joy alive?
choices: Sugar works better on a schedule
Variety and spacing slow adaptation's erasure
Favorites should be eaten only yearly
items.correctAnswer: Variety and spacing slow adaptation's erasure
items.correctExplanation: Correct. Adaptation feeds on repetition; variety starves it. Spacing pleasures keeps each occurrence surprising — the same dessert, un-dulled.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that variety and spacing slow adaptation's erasure. Daily repetition trains the thrill away; rotation preserves novelty. Design your pleasures with gaps and they keep paying.
items.lessonContent:
Repetition trains thrill away; rotation preserves it.
Spacing is savoring made structural.
Novelty can be scheduled, not just stumbled upon.
Same pleasures, arranged wisely, pay repeatedly.
Share this: rotate one daily pleasure this week.

items.title: The Comparison Diet
items.question: After unfollowing luxury influencers, Ana felt richer on the same salary. What changed?
choices: Her comparison set shrank to real life
items.correctAnswer: Her comparison set shrank to real life
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Same salary, saner yardstick. Feeds curate impossible reference points; removing them lets ordinary sufficiency register again.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is her comparison set shrank to real life. Nothing material moved — the measuring stick did. Comparison diets work because baselines are built from inputs, and inputs are editable.
items.lessonContent:
Baselines are built from daily inputs.
Curated feeds manufacture impossible yardsticks.
Sufficiency registers once comparison quiets.
Edit inputs; the baseline follows.
Share this: unfollow one account that taxes your contentment.

items.title: The Set Point
items.question: Twin studies suggest people have happiness 'set points' they drift back toward. What is the most hopeful accurate reading?
choices: Effort is useless, so abandon all growth
Set points are fixed and identical for everyone
Habits can nudge the range even if gravity pulls home
items.correctAnswer: Habits can nudge the range even if gravity pulls home
items.correctExplanation: Right. Set points describe gravity, not prison — practices like gratitude, exercise, and connection measurably shift the band. Drift home, but renovate home.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that habits can nudge the range even if gravity pulls home. Heritability is not immutability. The hopeful science: sustained practices move baselines modestly but really.
items.lessonContent:
Gravity describes pull, not prison.
Heritable is not immutable.
Sustained practices shift baselines for real.
Renovate home instead of fighting the drift.
Share this: pick one baseline habit for the next month.

items.title: The Anticipation Bonus
items.question: Research finds people often enjoy looking forward to trips more than the trips themselves. Where is the practical lesson?
choices: Cancel all trips and only imagine them
Never plan anything to avoid disappointment
items.correctAnswer: Stretch and savor anticipation deliberately
items.correctExplanation: Correct. Anticipation is free happiness paid in advance — plan early, countdown visibly, discuss eagerly. The wait can be designed as part of the gift.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to stretch and savor anticipation deliberately. Imagining-only misses the trip's own joys; the lesson is addition, not substitution. Countdowns, planning nights, and shared excitement are happiness with no price.
items.lessonContent:
Anticipation is happiness paid in advance.
Countdowns convert waiting into savoring.
Plan early and discuss eagerly — it counts double.
The wait is designable part of every gift.
Share this: start a countdown for something small and sweet.

items.title: The Giving High
items.question: Spending $20 on a friend reliably lifts mood more than spending it on oneself in experiments. Why would giving beat getting?
choices: Giving dodges adaptation by connecting rather than acquiring
items.correctAnswer: Giving dodges adaptation by connecting rather than acquiring
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Acquisitions join the baseline; connections refresh meaning. Giving spends money on relationship, which adaptation erodes far more slowly.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is that giving dodges adaptation by connecting rather than acquiring. Objects normalize; bonds compound. The $20 buys a story and a smile — assets the treadmill can't easily repossess.
items.lessonContent:
Connections compound; acquisitions normalize.
Stories and smiles resist the treadmill's repossession.
Prosocial spending buys meaning, not material.
Give small and often rather than grandly once.
Share this: spend a little on someone today and watch your mood.

items.title: The Nostalgia Trap
items.question: Ravi insists college was pure bliss, though his journals from then record heavy stress. What is memory doing?
choices: Rosy retrospection: fading negatives, keeping highlights
Recording the past with perfect fidelity
items.correctAnswer: Rosy retrospection: fading negatives, keeping highlights
items.correctExplanation: Right — rosy retrospection. Negatives fade faster than positives in recall, so the past glows. Compare with records, not feelings, before declaring eras golden.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is rosy retrospection: fading negatives, keeping highlights. Journals beat nostalgia because writing freezes the unedited mix. The past wasn't better — it is better remembered selectively.
items.lessonContent:
Memory edits: negatives fade, highlights keep.
Journals freeze the unedited mix — trust them over glow.
'Golden eras' are often just well-filtered ones.
Check records before ranking decades.
Share this: reread one old journal entry tonight.

items.title: The Enough Line
items.question: Which habit most directly resists the treadmill's pull?
choices: Defining 'enough' in advance and honoring it
items.correctAnswer: Defining 'enough' in advance and honoring it
items.correctExplanation: Correct. A predefined 'enough' line stops the baseline from drifting — arrival gets recognized instead of re-anchored. The treadmill needs a moving target; enough starves it.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is defining 'enough' in advance and honoring it. Every other option feeds the mechanism: bigger goals, upward comparison, scheduled upgrades. Enough is the only brake that works by design.
items.lessonContent:
'Enough' is a line drawn before arrival, not after.
Recognized arrivals satisfy; re-anchored ones don't.
Starve the treadmill of moving targets.
Honor the line publicly to make it stick.
Share this: declare one 'enough' out loud this week.

items.title: The Savoring Lens
items.question: Lingering over morning coffee — noticing aroma, warmth, taste — measurably lifts mood. What is savoring fighting?
choices: Adaptation's habit of making pleasures invisible
items.correctAnswer: Adaptation's habit of making pleasures invisible
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Daily pleasures go invisible fastest; savoring re-renders them. Attention is the anti-adaptation — the same cup, seen again for the first time.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is adaptation's habit of making pleasures invisible. The coffee never changed; perception dulled. Savoring restores the first-cup experience to cup number thousand.
items.lessonContent:
Daily pleasures go invisible fastest of all.
Attention re-renders the familiar as new.
Savoring is noticing with intent.
First-cup experiences can be reissued daily.
Share this: savor one routine thing fully tomorrow morning.

items.title: The Minimalist Dividend
items.question: After decluttering, Dana felt lighter and stopped browsing stores. What dividend did owning less pay?
choices: Fewer reference points for comparison and upkeep
items.correctAnswer: Fewer reference points for comparison and upkeep
items.correctExplanation: Right. Fewer possessions mean fewer comparison triggers and fewer maintenance taxes on attention. Lightness is the felt absence of treadmill fuel.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is fewer reference points for comparison and upkeep. Each object is a comparison candidate and a chore. Decluttering removes both at once — the dividend is attention returned.
items.lessonContent:
Objects are comparison candidates and chores at once.
Fewer things mean fewer baselines to defend.
Lightness is attention returned to its owner.
Decluttering removes treadmill fuel by the bag.
Share this: remove five objects and notice the quiet.

items.title: The Honeymoon Clock
items.question: New relationships glow; then ordinary days arrive and couples call it fading love. What is usually fading?
choices: Novelty — while deeper attachment can be growing
items.correctAnswer: Novelty — while deeper attachment can be growing
items.correctExplanation: Correct. The glow was novelty; its fade is adaptation, not verdict. Couples who mistake calm for loss chase new sparks instead of building warmth.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is novelty, while deeper attachment can be growing. Ordinary days are the relationship maturing, not dying. Measure warmth and trust, not butterflies — caterpillars were never the pet.
items.lessonContent:
Novelty fades by design; attachment grows by practice.
Calm is maturation, not malfunction.
Measure trust and warmth, not butterflies.
New sparks entertain; built warmth sustains.
Share this: thank a partner for one ordinary-day kindness.
